Yes, services like these can be bought on a multiyear basis, but only with the right determination and a cancellation structure. It is not the same thing as a base year with options.

The difference. RFO FAR 17.102 defines a multiyear contract as one that buys more than one and up to five program years of requirements without exercising an option for each later year. Later years depend on appropriations, and the contractor can be paid a cancellation charge if funds are not provided. A multiple-year contract with options commits only the base period, and the Government decides each year whether to exercise.

Authority. DFARS 217.103-171 implements 10 U.S.C. 3531. The head of the agency may enter into multiyear contracts of up to five years for covered services, even though O&M funds are annual. Covered services include operation, maintenance and support of installations and base services such as grounds maintenance and refuse collection. Before award the head of the agency must determine in writing that:
- the requirement will continue through the contract period,
- performance requires a substantial initial investment in plant or equipment, or substantial contingent liabilities for a specialized workforce, and
- a multiyear contract encourages effective competition and promotes economies in operations.
The $24 million equipment investment supports the second finding. Above $900 million, specific statutory authority would also be required (217.103-171(d)). AFARS 5117.103-171 points to Appendix GG for Army delegation, so I confirm who signs with our contracting policy office.

Contract terms. The contract uses FAR 52.217-2, plus 52.222-43 if the Service Contract Labor Standards apply. Funds obligated at award must cover the first fiscal year plus potential cancellation and termination costs, or the full period (17.104-4).

Notice. The ceiling is far below the $200 million congressional notice trigger. No further competition. 10 U.S.C. 4022(f)(2) allows a follow-on production contract or transaction to the participants without competitive procedures if competitive procedures were used to select the parties for the prototype transaction and the participants successfully completed the prototype project. Under (f)(3) and (f)(4), a successfully completed subproject within a consortium can qualify even if the consortium's other work is unfinished. Risks I raise:
- The record. A thin record on the original competition or on successful completion is the most exposed point if the award is challenged.
- The vehicle. Under 4022(f)(5) the follow-on may be an OT or a procurement contract. In my view, choosing a FAR-based contract brings the other procurement requirements, such as certified cost or pricing data, even though the competition requirement is satisfied.
